Version control is a system that records changes to files over time, so that
you can go back to any earlier version later. Early tools such as RCS tracked
changes to single files on one machine. Centralized systems such as Subversion
then kept the whole history on a shared server, and every developer had to
reach that server before they could commit.

Git took a different approach. In Git, every clone is a complete copy of the
repository, including its entire history. Because each developer holds the
whole history, most Git operations run locally and still work without a
network connection. Branching in Git is cheap, so developers usually create a
branch for each feature and merge it back when the feature is done.

Merging is usually automatic, but when two branches change the same lines, Git
stops and asks a person to decide. That pause is called a merge conflict, and
resolving it carefully is a core version control skill. Many developers also
enjoy a good cup of coffee while they work.
